# Contribution Acknowledgment

## When to use this

Send one for every contribution of $250 or more, without exception, and as a
matter of practice for every contribution of any size.

The statutory trigger is 26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8): a donor may claim no deduction
for a contribution of $250 or more unless they hold a contemporaneous written
acknowledgment from the Kingdom containing what the statute requires. The duty to
hold it is the donor's. The ability to supply it belongs to the Kingdom alone, and
a donor whose deduction is disallowed because the Kingdom sent nothing, or sent
the wrong words, or sent it in April, does not give again — and tells the people
who introduced them.

Use the quid pro quo variant instead wherever the donor received anything back
worth more than a token: a banquet ticket, a retreat place, an auction lot, a
concert seat, a book of substance. That is a separate obligation under
26 U.S.C. § 6115, it attaches above $75 rather than $250, and it carries its own
penalty.

Do not use either form for a pledge. A promise to give is not a contribution and
must not be acknowledged as one until the funds or the property actually arrive.
Do not use them for contributed services, which are never deductible, though a
volunteer's unreimbursed out-of-pocket expenses may be and have their own
acknowledgment requirements.

## Before you send

- [ ] **The contribution is recorded in the Register of Contributions, Grants and
      Disbursements,** and the letter is generated from that entry rather than
      written from memory or from a note on a desk.
- [ ] **The funds or the property have actually been received.** Not pledged, not
      promised, not in transit.
- [ ] **The date is the date of the contribution, not the date of the letter.**
      For a cheque, the date mailed; for a card or electronic transfer, the date
      charged or transferred; for property, the date of delivery.
- [ ] **The donor is named exactly as they will appear on their return** —
      individual, couple, trust, company, or donor-advised fund. Where a
      donor-advised fund or a family foundation made the payment, the donor is the
      fund or foundation, not the individual who directed it, and the letter must
      not tell that individual they made a deductible gift.
- [ ] **Someone has answered the goods-or-services question honestly** and in
      writing before the letter is drafted. This is the element that most often
      destroys a deduction, and the answer is not always no.
- [ ] **No dollar value appears for any non-cash gift.** The Kingdom describes
      what it received; the donor and their appraiser value it.
- [ ] **The gift was not earmarked for a named individual.** A payment routed
      through the Kingdom to a particular person is not a deductible contribution
      and must not be acknowledged as one.
- [ ] **The letter is going out within thirty days,** and in every case before
      31 January following the year of the gift.
- [ ] **Nothing in the letter cites 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A) or describes the
      Kingdom as a "508(c)(1)(A) organisation."** See the Notes. That phrase on a
      donor letter is a liability, not a credential.
- [ ] **The letter is signed by an officer with authority** and a copy is filed
      against the register entry.

## The letter — cash contribution, nothing given in return

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD]

[DATE OF LETTER]

[DONOR FULL NAME, AS IT WILL APPEAR ON THE DONOR'S RETURN]
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY, STATE, ZIP]

Dear [MR./MS./MX./DR. SURNAME]:

On behalf of Apex Kingdom, thank you for your contribution. [ONE
SENTENCE, SPECIFIC AND SINCERE, ABOUT WHAT IT SUPPORTS.]

This letter is your receipt for tax purposes. Please keep it with your
records.

     Donor:                [DONOR FULL NAME]
     Date of contribution: [DATE RECEIVED]
     Amount received:      $[AMOUNT]
     Form:                 [cash / check no. 0000 / electronic transfer /
                            credit card]
     Reference:            [FIN RECORD NUMBER]

No goods or services were provided by Apex Kingdom in consideration for
this contribution.

[USE THE FOLLOWING SENTENCE INSTEAD OF THE ONE ABOVE ONLY WHERE THE ONLY
THING THE DONOR RECEIVED WAS AN INTANGIBLE RELIGIOUS BENEFIT: No goods or
services were provided by Apex Kingdom in consideration for this
contribution other than intangible religious benefits.]

Apex Kingdom is a church within the meaning of 26 U.S.C.
§ 170(b)(1)(A)(i) and is exempt from federal income tax under 26 U.S.C.
§ 501(c)(3). [Employer Identification Number: [EIN].]

Please retain this acknowledgment. The Internal Revenue Code requires a
donor to have a written acknowledgment of this kind in hand before filing
the return on which the contribution is claimed, and we are unable to
supply it after that point in a way that helps you. If anything above is
incorrect, please tell us and we will issue a corrected acknowledgment.

With gratitude,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]
```

## Variant — non-cash contribution

Replace the receipt block above with the following. Change nothing else.

```
     Donor:                [DONOR FULL NAME]
     Date of contribution: [DATE OF DELIVERY]
     Property received:    [DESCRIPTION WITHOUT VALUATION — e.g., "one
                            upright piano, Baldwin, serial no. 000000,
                            in working order" / "42 folding chairs" /
                            "one 2014 Ford Transit van, VIN 0000000"]
     Reference:            [FIN RECORD NUMBER]

Apex Kingdom does not assign a value to contributed property. The
determination of value, and the substantiation required for it, are the
donor's responsibility and that of the donor's own advisers.
```

## Variant — quid pro quo contribution (26 U.S.C. § 6115)

Use this where the donor paid more than $75 and received goods or services in
return. The statement below must be given at solicitation or on receipt.

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD]

[DATE OF LETTER]

[DONOR FULL NAME]
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY, STATE, ZIP]

Dear [MR./MS./MX./DR. SURNAME]:

Thank you for your support of [THE EVENT OR PROGRAMME]. This letter is
your receipt.

     Donor:                  [DONOR FULL NAME]
     Date of payment:        [DATE]
     Total amount paid:      $[TOTAL]
     Reference:              [FIN RECORD NUMBER]

     Goods or services
     provided in return:     [DESCRIBE — e.g., "admission for two to the
                              Founders' Dinner on 14 March 2026,
                              including dinner and entertainment"]

     Good-faith estimate of
     their value:            $[VALUE]

     Amount paid in excess
     of the value received:  $[TOTAL MINUS VALUE]

For federal income tax purposes, the amount of your contribution that is
deductible as a charitable contribution is limited to the excess of the
amount of money you paid over the value of the goods or services provided
to you by Apex Kingdom. The figures above are stated so that you have
that information; whether and to what extent you may claim a deduction is
a matter for you and your tax adviser.

[WHERE ANY PART OF THE PAYMENT WAS PURELY A GIFT AND THE DONOR DECLINED
THE BENEFIT IN WRITING BEFORE THE EVENT, SAY SO HERE AND ADJUST THE
FIGURES ACCORDINGLY.]

Apex Kingdom is a church within the meaning of 26 U.S.C.
§ 170(b)(1)(A)(i) and is exempt from federal income tax under 26 U.S.C.
§ 501(c)(3). [Employer Identification Number: [EIN].]

Please retain this statement with your records. If anything above is
incorrect, please tell us and we will issue a corrected statement.

With gratitude,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]
```

## Notes

**The three required elements, and why the third is where letters fail.** Under
26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(8)(B) the acknowledgment must state the amount of cash and
describe (but not value) any property other than cash contributed; state whether
the Kingdom provided any goods or services in consideration for the contribution;
and, where it did, describe them and give a good-faith estimate of their value —
or, where the only thing provided was an intangible religious benefit, say that
instead.

The first two are easy and almost always present. The third is a sentence that has
to appear even when the answer is nothing, and its absence is fatal. *Durden v.
Commissioner*, T.C. Memo. 2012-140, is the case to keep in mind: a couple made
substantial cash gifts to their church by cheque, every one of them documented and
none of them disputed. The church's first letter omitted the no-goods-or-services
statement. The church sent a corrected letter with the statement in it — after the
return was filed. The deduction was disallowed in full. Nobody had done anything
wrong except leave out one sentence and fix it a month too late.

**"Contemporaneous" is a hard deadline that falls earlier than anyone expects.**
Section 170(f)(8)(C) defines it: the donor must obtain the acknowledgment on or
before the *earlier* of the date they file the return for the year of the
contribution, or the due date, including extensions, for filing that return. A
donor who files on 3 February has closed the window on 3 February. An
acknowledgment sent in April for a gift made the previous May is often already
worthless, and a corrected one sent after the filing is worthless as a matter of
law however accurate it is.

This is why the practice rule is thirty days from receipt, and 31 January at the
very latest. There is no relief provision, no reasonable-cause exception, and no
way to cure it afterwards. It is the cheapest obligation in this system to meet
and the only one that cannot be repaired.

**The $250 test is per contribution, not per year.** Separate gifts of less than
$250 each are not aggregated. Fifty-two weekly envelope gifts of $40 need no
acknowledgment under § 170(f)(8), though the donor still needs a bank record or a
written communication from the Kingdom showing its name, the date, and the amount
for *any* cash gift, whatever its size (26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(17)). A cancelled
cheque alone does not satisfy § 170(f)(8) for a gift of $250 or more.

An annual statement is good practice and good stewardship, and it may be used to
acknowledge a year's giving in one document — provided every single contribution
of $250 or more is separately listed with its own date and amount and its own
goods-or-services statement, rather than folded into a total. A single figure for
the year does not substantiate anything.

**Quid pro quo is a different statute with a lower threshold.** Section 6115
applies to any payment over $75 made partly as a contribution and partly for goods
or services. It requires a written statement that informs the donor that the
deductible amount is limited to the excess of what they paid over the value of
what they received, and that gives a good-faith estimate of that value. The
statement must be made at solicitation or at receipt. Failure carries a penalty
under 26 U.S.C. § 6714 — assessed per contribution, capped per event or mailing —
and, more to the point, leaves every attendee at the dinner holding a receipt that
does not do what they think it does.

Two exclusions are worth knowing. Where the only benefit is token or de minimis in
the amounts the IRS publishes and adjusts annually, no § 6115 statement is
required. And § 6115 does not apply where the only thing provided is an intangible
religious benefit — which is why a payment for a place at a retreat consisting
solely of worship, prayer, and instruction is treated differently from a payment
for a banquet.

**The intangible religious benefit sentence, and one caution about it.** The
statutory language at § 170(f)(8)(B)(iii) covers goods or services consisting
solely of intangible religious benefits provided by an organization organized
exclusively for religious purposes. Used correctly it is exactly right for
sacramental and liturgical settings — a Mass intention, a place at a retreat, the
benefit of prayer.

The caution is specific to this institution. The Charter describes the Kingdom
simultaneously as a religious body, a tribal government, and a charitable trust.
"Organized exclusively for religious purposes" is a phrase an examiner reads
against the organisation's own governing instrument, and the Charter as it stands
does not obviously say that. Use the intangible-religious-benefit sentence where
it is plainly true of the transaction, and prefer the ordinary
no-goods-or-services statement everywhere else, because the ordinary statement
carries no such question with it. This is one of several reasons the interpretive
declaration contemplated at step 10 of the programme in `01-LEGAL-POSTURE` is
worth doing.

**Describe property; never value it.** For non-cash gifts the Kingdom states what
it received and nothing more. Valuation is the donor's responsibility and their
appraiser's, and an organisation that supplies a number has taken on a risk that
belongs to somebody else and has given the donor something to point at when the
number is challenged. Two related duties follow the property itself: for a noncash
deduction over $5,000 the Kingdom signs the donee acknowledgment section of the
donor's Form 8283, which acknowledges receipt only and is not agreement with the
value; and if the Kingdom disposes of such property within three years it must file
Form 8282 within 125 days of the disposition.

**Never write "508(c)(1)(A)" on a donor letter.** Section 508(c)(1)(A) excepts
churches from the requirement in § 508(a) to *apply* for recognition of exemption.
That is its entire content. It is not a grant of exemption, it is not a status an
organisation obtains or is issued, and there is no such thing as a "508(c)(1)(A)
organisation" — the packages sold online under that name are a recognised fraud
vector. A donor letter citing it tells any accountant who reads it that the
Kingdom's tax posture came from the internet, and a donor whose preparer forms that
view will not give again.

The accurate statement is the one in the template, and it is stronger: the Kingdom
is a church described in 26 U.S.C. § 170(b)(1)(A)(i) and exempt under
§ 501(c)(3). A church is exempt without applying and contributions to it are
deductible, and neither fact requires a determination letter. Do not claim to hold
a determination letter unless one has actually been issued; where a donor's adviser
asks for one, say plainly that the Kingdom is a church and has not sought a
determination letter, which is a complete and unremarkable answer.

**Two things this letter must never do.** It must not tell the donor that their
contribution *is* deductible, or how much they may deduct. State the facts the
statute requires and let the donor and their adviser reach the conclusion; a
charity that opines on a donor's return is guessing about facts it does not have.
And it must not acknowledge a gift earmarked for a named individual as a charitable
contribution, however sympathetic the case. A payment the Kingdom is merely passing
through to a person the donor chose is not a contribution to the Kingdom, and
acknowledging it as one is a misstatement in a document the donor will file with a
federal return.

**Do not backdate, and do not quietly re-issue.** Where an error is found, issue a
corrected acknowledgment that says on its face that it corrects the acknowledgment
of [date], keep both against the register entry, and record the correction. Where a
contribution is returned or refunded, withdraw the acknowledgment in writing so the
donor does not claim a deduction for a gift they no longer made.
